title: architecture-standards-consolidated-guidelines-and-adrs-2026-03-04
author: Marcus Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and standards across API, coding, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance disciplines. It also indexes active decision records (ADRs) that govern exceptions and evolution. The goal is to provide a single, authoritative reference for engineers and architects implementing production inference services.

Audience
- Software engineers and ML engineers building services on Redwood's platform
- Platform and infra teams responsible for service reliability and cost
- Security and compliance partners evaluating designs

Scope
Applies to all public and internal services that are part of Redwood Inference's hosted, dedicated, or private product lines, including: runtime services, orchestrator components, telemetry pipelines, and customer-facing APIs.

1) API Standards

Overview
APIs must be stable, discoverable, and predictable. Use REST/JSON for control-plane operations and gRPC/streaming for high-throughput internal RPCs where latency and throughput requirements demand it.

Principles
- Explicit versioning: /v1/, /v2/ in the path. Breaking changes must result in a new major version.
- Backwards compatibility: Additive fields only; deprecate with 90-day notice and runtime warnings in responses.
- Consistent error model: standardized error envelope (see example).

Error schema (JSON):
{
  "error": {
    "code": "string (machine_readable)",
    "message": "string (human_readable)",
    "details": ["optional array of strings or structured info"],
    "request_id": "uuid"
  }
}

HTTP and Status Codes
- 200: OK (successful request)
- 202: Accepted (async work started e.g., model load)
- 400: Bad Request (validation)
- 401/403: Auth (use RBAC & scoped API keys)
- 404: Not Found
- 409: Conflict (concurrent updates)
- 429: Rate limited (include Retry-After header)
- 500/502/503/504: Server errors (include request_id and trace_id)

Pagination and Limits
- Cursor-based pagination for list APIs. Responses include: next_cursor, page_size.
- Max page_size: 1000. Default: 100.

API Design Guidelines
- Resource naming: kebab-case, plural resources (e.g., /models, /deployments).
- Use query parameters for filtering and POST for complex searches (/search instead of GET with huge query string).
- Idempotency: support idempotency keys for non-idempotent POSTs (Idempotency-Key header).
- Rate limiting: per-account and per-token limits. Return 429 with X-RateLimit-* headers.

Example: Model creation (POST /v1/models) payload
{
  "name": "gpt-neoxt-20b-custom",
  "revision": "2026-02-15",
  "quantization_profile": "q4_0",
  "metadata": {"framework": "transformers", "base_model": "gpt-neoxt"}
}

2) Coding Standards

Languages in primary use: Go (backend services), Python (inference harnesses, evals), TypeScript (console front-end).

Common rules
- Formatting and linting enforced via pre-commit and CI.
  - Go: gofmt, golangci-lint (enable govet, staticcheck, gosimple).
  - Python: black, isort, ruff, mypy (strict mode for new modules).
  - TypeScript: eslint (recommended ruleset), prettier.
- Tests: every public package/service must have unit tests and integration tests for critical paths. Coverage minimum: 60% for libraries, 80% for core infra packages.
- Logging: structured JSON logs with keys: ts, level, service, module, request_id, trace_id, msg. Avoid logging PII.
- Secrets: never hardcode secrets; use KMS-backed secret manager; unit tests use mocked secret providers.
- Code review: minimum one reviewer; for infra changes affecting multiple services, require two reviewers and an approver from eng-platform.

Code layout examples
- Go services: internal/ (private packages), api/ (public handlers), cmd/ (binaries), pkg/ (shared cross-service libs).
- Python packages: src/<package>/, tests/, integration_tests/.

3) Infrastructure Standards

IaC and Environment Parity
- Terraform is the canonical source for cloud infra; modules must be published to the internal registry. Reuse modules for VPC, subnets, DNS, IAM.
- Environments: dev (non-prod), staging (pre-prod), prod. Deployments should be automated via CI with environment-specific variables pulled from a secure parameter store.

Networking and Security
- VPC per environment with enforced flow logs. Use private subnets for compute; NAT gateways for controlled egress.
- Use service accounts with least privilege. All roles must be documented in IAM manifests.
- KMS/HSM for key management; envelope encryption recommended for customer data.

Tagging and Ownership
- All cloud resources require tags: service, team, cost-center, environment, owner_email.

Cost & Capacity
- GPU instance types: use curated lists in gpu-fleet-and-capacity guidelines; prefer integer GPU counts per pool.
- Autoscaling must include burst/backpressure controls to avoid noisy neighbor and runaway costs.

Release & Rollback
- Deploys follow CI -> canary (5-10% traffic for 10 minutes) -> gradual rollout -> full. Automatic rollback on critical SLO degradation or error spikes.

4) Model-Serving Standards

Model packaging and versioning
- Models are first-class artifacts with provenance metadata: source_checkpoint, commit_hash, tokenizer_spec, training_config, quantization_profile.
- Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH for model revisions; model aliasing allowed (e.g., best-effort stable aliases).

Deployment patterns
- Each model deployment exposes: control-plane endpoint (management) and dataplane endpoint (inference). Dataplane endpoints must be behind a proxy with TLS termination and mTLS for internal clients.
- Default deployment flavor: autoscaled GPU pool with continuous batching and prefix KV cache.

Resource constraints and limits
- Max sequence length default: 4,096 tokens; models requiring longer sequences must justify and obtain approval.
- Default per-request token limit: 2,048 for hosted API; Dedicated/private customers may opt for custom limits.

Performance knobs
- Batching: prefer dynamic batching with max_batch_size tuned per model.
- Quantization profiles: pre-approved profiles maintained in quantization-profiles directory (q8_0, q4_0, q4_1).
- KV cache: enable for chat/streaming endpoints; eviction policy LFU with time-based TTL.

Observability for Model Serving
- Key metrics: model_load_time, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, tokens_per_second, batch_size_histogram, cache_hit_rate, gpu_utilization. Emit with labels: model_name, revision, flavor, region, pool_id.

Quality and Regression Controls
- Every model rollout must include a smoke eval run against a canonical prompt set (see prompt-sets-and-benchmarks) and compare quality metrics to baseline.
- If quality regression > 2 points (on agreed metric) or latency regression > 15% at p95, block rollout.

5) Observability Standards

Logs
- Centralized JSON logs to the ELK stack (or equivalent). Logs must include request_id and trace_id for correlation. Sensitive fields must be redacted before ingestion.

Tracing
- Distributed tracing using OpenTelemetry. All services must propagate trace_id and span_id. Sampling: 100% for error traces, 1-5% for successful traces.

Metrics
- Metrics emitted via Prometheus exposition format. Use stable metric names and labels. Avoid cardinality explosion: label cardinality limit per metric: 100.
- Standard metric prefixes: service_*, infra_*, model_*.

Dashboards & Alerts
- Dashboard templates are in dashboards-and-alerts. Each service must have: Overview (latency, error rate, throughput), Capacity (utilization), Cost (tokens/sec * cost_per_token), and recent deployments.
- Alerting thresholds:
  - P95 latency increase > 30% over baseline for 10m -> page oncall (severity P1).
  - Error rate > 1% sustained over 5m -> page oncall (severity P1).
  - SLO burn rate > 2x for 1h -> page oncall.

6) Performance Standards and Benchmarks

Service SLOs
- Availability SLO (control plane): 99.95% monthly.
- Dataplane inference SLOs (per model flavor): Default p95 latency target: <= 150ms for short-text workloads (<=128 tokens) on production GPU pools; for long context workloads (>=1024 tokens) targets are negotiated per-model.
- Throughput SLO: capacity planning target to sustain 95th percentile request rate with <10% queuing.

Benchmarking
- All changes that touch the serving runtime or kernel selection must run the benchmarking-and-perf-suite. Benchmarks must include: cold-start model_load_time, steady-state throughput (tokens/sec), latency percentiles (p50/p90/p95/p99), and memory/GPU utilization.
- Bench results must be published with artifacts and raw logs attached to the change PR.

Performance Regression Process
1. Automated perf tests run in CI against a representative hardware fixture.
2. If regression detected (>5% p95 increase or >10% throughput drop), PR is blocked and owner must provide root cause and mitigation.
3. For borderline regressions, run expanded tests on staging fleet; if confirmed, revert unless approved by infra-performance lead.

7) Decision Records (ADRs) and Exceptions

ADR Index (active and recent)
- ADR-2024-01: Standardize on gRPC for internal high-throughput RPCs — rationale: lower latency and efficient streaming. Owner: Eng-Platform. Status: accepted.
- ADR-2025-03: Quantization profile defaults (q4_0 for latency-sensitive models) — rationale: cost-performance tradeoff. Owner: Applied ML. Status: accepted.
- ADR-2025-11: Default P95 inference latency target for short-text workloads — rationale: customer SLA expectations and hardware capability. Owner: Eng-SRE. Status: accepted.
- ADR-2026-02: Model artifact provenance and mandatory metadata fields — Owner: Research/Applied ML. Status: accepted.

How to author an ADR
1. Create a brief ADR document in architecture-and-standards/decision-records with proposal, alternatives, pros/cons, and proposed owner.
2. Notify reviewers (eng-platform, eng-sre, applied-ml) and allow a 7-business-day comment period.
3. Accepted ADRs are added to the index and must include migration guidance if they introduce breaking changes.

Exceptions and Safe Paths
- Requests for exceptions must include: justification, risk assessment, rollback plan, and proposed observability. Exceptions approved by Eng Directors are valid for 90 days and must be renewed.

8) Onboarding & Change Process

New Service Checklist
- Register service in service catalog (owner, SLOs, runbook link).
- Create initial dashboards and alerts from templates.
- Add IAM policies and tags.
- Run end-to-end smoke tests against staging.

Change Review
- All infra, runtime, or model-serving changes require: PR with benchmark artifacts, perf test results, and security review if applicable.
- Breaking API changes require deprecation notice and migration guide.

9) Ownership and Escalation

Ownership matrix (example)
- API design & SDKs: Eng-Developer-Experience
- Runtime kernel & scheduling: Eng-Serving-Runtime
- Fleet capacity & autoscaling: Eng-SRE
- Model onboarding & quantization: Applied ML

Escalation
- Oncall -> service owner -> eng-platform -> eng-sre director. For incidents affecting customer SLAs, page product/CS and legal as required.

Appendices

A. Example CI perf job snippet (YAML)
- job: perf-ci
  image: perf-runner:stable
  steps:
    - run: ./bench/run_bench.sh --model $MODEL --fixture staging-1-gpu
    - run: ./bench/compare_baseline.py --artifact new_run.json --baseline baseline.json

B. Metric naming recommendations
- service_http_requests_total (labels: service, route, method, code)
- model_inference_tokens_total (labels: model_name, revision, flavor)

C. Quick links
- dashboards-and-alerts templates
- quantization-profiles directory
- prompt-sets-and-benchmarks for rollout checks

Contact
For questions or suggested edits, open a PR against this doc or contact the owner: marcus.chen@redwood-inference.com.
